label: Institution
name: Church of King Charles the Martyr, Royal Tunbridge Wells
summary:
The Church of King Charles the Martyr in Royal Tunbridge Wells, Kent, England, is a rare example of a Church of England church dedicated to King Charles I (1600-1649) — the only English monarch ever executed, who was declared a martyr by the Church of England shortly after his execution and inserted into the Book of Common Prayer calendar as 'King Charles the Martyr' (January 30) in a special commemoration that was observed until 1859. The church's dedication reflects the Royalist religious culture of the Restoration period and Tunbridge Wells' development as a fashionable spa town under Charles II.

King Charles I's execution on January 30, 1649, by the Parliamentarian/Puritan government was an event of extraordinary political and religious impact. The 'martyrdom' narrative was constructed immediately by Royalist propagandists — particularly through the 'Eikon Basilike' (published the day of his execution, supposedly written by Charles himself), which became one of the best-selling books of the century and portrayed Charles as a suffering Christian king martyred for his faith and the Church of England. The Church of England formally commemorated him as a martyr from 1662 (Restoration) until 1859 (when the commemoration was quietly removed).

Tunbridge Wells' development as a Royal spa town began when Henrietta Maria (Charles II's wife) visited the chalybeate springs in 1630, and the town expanded dramatically under Charles II — hence 'Royal Tunbridge Wells.' The Church of King Charles the Martyr (built 1678-1682, expanded 1690) was dedicated to Charles I in the context of Restoration Royalism, making it an architectural expression of the divine-right monarchy ideology that the Civil War had challenged and the Restoration had reasserted.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: The Church of King Charles the Martyr Tunbridge Wells — one of England's rare churches dedicated to the executed king whose martyrdom narrative shaped Restoration Anglican Royalism, built during the spa town's Restoration development — is historically significant as an architectural monument of the English Civil War's religious aftermath.
